title: Jerez
description: The Sherry triangle: white albariza soils, flor yeast and soleras that blend wines across generations.
L: Explain the role of the two winds

Sherry comes from the area around three towns in Andalusia, south-west Spain: Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María and Sanlúcar de Barrameda, the Sherry triangle. The DO is Jerez-Xérès-Sherry, Spain's oldest, from 1933. Wines must age in one of the three towns; Sanlúcar's is called Manzanilla.

The best vineyards sit on albariza, a brilliant white soil with up to 40% chalk, formed from ancient marine algae. It soaks up winter rain like a sponge and forms a crust in summer that slows evaporation. Its whiteness reflects sunlight onto the vines. Named vineyard areas, pagos, like Macharnudo, Carrascal and Miraflores, sit on it.
It stores winter rain and reflects sunlight
Its chalk holds water and its whiteness reflects light.

Jerez is hot, with over 300 sunny days a year. Two winds matter. The Poniente, from the Atlantic, is cool and humid, favouring flor yeast in the cellars. The Levante, from the east, is hot and dry, concentrating grapes but stressing flor. Bodegas are built with high ceilings and thick walls, often facing the Poniente.
The Poniente wind brings humidity that helps flor grow.
Yes. It's cool and humid, from the Atlantic.
Sherry comes from the triangle of Jerez, El Puerto and Sanlúcar
Albariza stores water and reflects light
The humid Poniente and dry Levante shape vineyard and cellar

Palomino Fino is about 95% of the vineyards. It's neutral, low in acidity and sugar, giving base wines of about 11 to 12.5%. Its neutrality is a strength: Sherry's flavours come from ageing, flor and oxygen, not from the grape.

Pedro Ximénez, PX, and Moscatel are used for sweet wines and for sweetening blends. They're often dried in the sun on mats, asoleo, for one to three weeks, becoming almost raisins. Much PX comes from nearby Montilla-Moriles, which is allowed in Sherry. Fermentation is stopped early by fortification, keeping huge sugar levels.
Match each grape to its use.
Pedro Ximénez is one of the sweetest wines in the world, often over 400 g/l of sugar. Pour it over vanilla ice cream.
Why is Palomino ideal for Sherry?
Its neutrality lets ageing create the flavours
Flor and oxygen write the flavour.
Palomino, about 95%, gives neutral base wines
PX and Moscatel are dried in the sun for sweet wines
Sherry's flavour comes from ageing, not the grape
Explain the classification of base wines

After fermentation, base wines are tasted and classified. The finest, palest are fortified to about 15 to 15.5% and put in barrels, botas, filled about five-sixths. A film of yeast, flor, grows on the surface. It protects the wine from oxygen and feeds on alcohol and glycerol, producing acetaldehyde: bready, nutty, saline aromas. This is biological ageing.

Sherry ages in a solera: rows of barrels of different ages. Wine is drawn from the oldest, the solera, a process called saca, never more than about a third at a time; by law, no more than 40% a year. It's replaced from the next oldest, the first criadera, and so on, a process called rocío. Young wine enters the youngest criadera. The result is a consistent blend of many ages.
Put the solera's movements in order.
Draw from the oldest tier, the saca
Refill it from the first criadera
Refill the first criadera from the second
Add young wine to the youngest tier
Wine moves step by step from young to old.

Base wines are classified by taste. Light, delicate wines are marked for Fino and Manzanilla, fortified to 15%. Fuller wines go to Oloroso, fortified to 17%, where flor can't live. Some wines change paths during ageing, losing their flor and becoming Amontillado or Palo Cortado.
At what strength can flor no longer survive?
At 17%, flor dies; the wine ages with oxygen.
Flor protects Fino and adds bready, saline notes
The solera blends many ages through saca and rocío
Base wines are classified for Fino or Oloroso

Fino ages under flor, usually at least two years, often more, in Jerez or El Puerto. It's pale, bone dry, about 15%, with almond, bread dough, chamomile and a saline edge. El Puerto's Finos, closer to the sea, are often lighter. Fino is best fresh: once opened, drink within a few days.

Manzanilla is Fino aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, at the mouth of the Guadalquivir. Cooler, more humid sea air keeps flor thicker all year, giving lighter, more saline, delicate wines with chamomile notes; manzanilla means chamomile in Spanish. Manzanilla Pasada is an older Manzanilla, with more nutty depth.
Why is flor thicker in Sanlúcar de Barrameda?
Sea air at the river mouth keeps flor thriving.

En rama, raw, means Sherry bottled with little or no filtration or fining, straight from the barrel. It's more intense and closer to the wine in the cask. Many bodegas release Fino and Manzanilla en rama seasonally, often in spring when flor is thickest. These are best drunk soon after bottling.
En rama: unfiltered, from the cask
Fino ages under flor: pale, dry, almond and bread
Manzanilla is Sanlúcar's lighter, more saline Fino
En rama Sherries are unfiltered and best fresh

Amontillado starts as a Fino under flor, then the flor fades or is killed by fortifying to about 17%, and the wine ages oxidatively. It's amber, dry, with hazelnut, toffee and saline notes. Palo Cortado is rare: a wine that loses its flor early, combining Amontillado's delicate aroma with Oloroso's richer body.

Oloroso, fragrant, is fortified to about 17% from the start, never has flor, and ages with oxygen for years. It darkens to mahogany, with walnut, leather, dried fruit and spice. It's naturally dry, despite seeming rich. As water evaporates, alcohol can rise to 20% or more.
Match each Sherry to its ageing.

Pedro Ximénez Sherry is black, syrupy and very sweet, with raisin, fig, coffee and liquorice. Moscatel is sweet and floral. Cream Sherry blends Oloroso with sweet wine; Pale Cream blends Fino with sweetening. Age statements, VOS, 20 years, and VORS, 30 years, mark very old Sherries.
Order these Sherries from palest to darkest.
Biological ageing keeps wine pale; oxidation and dried grapes darken it.
Amontillado and Palo Cortado combine flor and oxygen
Oloroso ages oxidatively and stays dry
PX and Cream are sweet; VOS and VORS mark old Sherry
Reading Sherry and eating with it

Sherry labels name the style: Fino, Manzanilla, Amontillado, Oloroso, Palo Cortado, Cream or PX. Look for en rama, an age statement like VOS or VORS, or 12 or 15 year old Sherry. Manzanilla always comes from Sanlúcar. Most Sherry has no vintage, being a solera blend; añada Sherries are rare single vintages.

Serve Fino and Manzanilla well chilled, 6 to 8 degrees, in a white wine glass; keep open bottles in the fridge and finish within a week. Amontillado and Palo Cortado at 12 to 14; Oloroso at 14 to 16; PX slightly cool. Oxidative styles keep for weeks once open.
Well chilled, and finished within a week
After years in an open bottle
Fino is delicate; serve it cold and fresh.

Fino and Manzanilla suit tapas: olives, almonds, jamón, fried fish, prawns. Amontillado suits soups, mushrooms and tricky vegetables like artichokes and asparagus. Oloroso suits stews, game and hard cheese. PX suits vanilla ice cream, blue cheese and chocolate.
Which foods suit Fino or Manzanilla?
Labels name the style and sometimes an age
Serve Fino cold and fresh; Oloroso cool
Fino with tapas, Amontillado with soups, PX with ice cream
Match each term to its meaning.
Not true. It's dry; sweet versions are blended.
By law, no more than ____% of a solera can be drawn per year.
Sherry comes from the triangle's albariza soils
Palomino becomes Fino under flor or Oloroso with oxygen
Each style suits a different dish
